A payment processor migration in August also caused failed card charges. brief.data: 212,400 active sponsorships as of Nov 1, 2026, across 23 country programs (e.g. Guatemala, Kenya, Bangladesh, Philippines). prompt:
I need the front end for Retention Lens. An in-house analysis tool built for the supporter-care department of a large international child-sponsorship charity to study why sponsors cancel and which groups of supporters are leaving.

Who's using it: Hana Lindqvist, a senior supporter-insights analyst in the supporter-care department. She is fluent in the charity's data and its reason codes, and she reports to the department director, who is not a data person.

What they're doing right now: Cancellations jumped in September and October, right after the monthly sponsorship gift went from $39 to $45. The director has to brief the executive team on Friday and wants to know if the increase caused the jump or if something else is going on. A payment processor migration in August also caused failed card charges. Hana is splitting cancellations by reason, how long the sponsor had given, how they signed up and which country program they support. She wants to separate deliberate cancellations from lapses caused by payment failures and find out whether long-tenured sponsors reacted differently from new ones.

What's in the system at this point: 212,400 active sponsorships as of Nov 1, 2026, across 23 country programs (e.g. Guatemala, Kenya, Bangladesh, Philippines). Monthly cancellations for Jan 2025–Oct 2026, averaging 2,150 per month, then 3,480 in September and 3,910 in October. 11 cancellation reason codes (e.g. FIN-HARDSHIP, PRICE-INCREASE, PAYMENT-FAILED-NO-RESPONSE, CHILD-LEFT-PROGRAM, NO-REASON). Sponsor attributes: tenure band (<1 yr, 1–3, 3–10, 10+), acquisition channel (TV, digital, event, church partner, peer referral), payment method (card, bank debit, check), age band and region. 6,240 failed card charges since the Aug 18 processor migration, 2,010 of them later recovered. Price-increase letters were sent in three waves on Aug 4, Aug 25 and Sep 15.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
